Migdal Effect in Dark Matter Direct Detection Experiments

Preprint: IPMU17-0100
Masahiro Ibe e-mail: ibe@icrr.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: ICRR, The University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba 277-8582, Japan Affiliation: Kavli IPMU (WPI), UTIAS, The University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba 277-8583, Japan    Wakutaka Nakano e-mail: m156077@icrr.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: ICRR, The University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba 277-8582, Japan    Yutaro Shoji e-mail: yshoji@icrr.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: ICRR, The University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba 277-8582, Japan    Kazumine Suzuki e-mail: ksuzuki@icrr.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: ICRR, The University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba 277-8582, Japan
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The elastic scattering of an atomic nucleus plays a central role in dark matter direct detection experiments. In those experiments, it is usually assumed that the atomic electrons around the nucleus of the target material immediately follow the motion of the recoil nucleus. In reality, however, it takes some time for the electrons to catch up, which results in ionization and excitation of the atoms. In previous studies, those effects are taken into account by using the so-called Migdal’s approach, in which the final state ionization/excitation are treated separately from the nuclear recoil. In this paper, we reformulate the Migdal’s approach so that the “atomic recoil” cross section is obtained coherently, where we make transparent the energy-momentum conservation and the probability conservation. We show that the final state ionization/excitation can enhance the detectability of rather light dark matter in the GeV mass range via the nuclear scattering. We also discuss the coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering, where the same effects are expected.

I Introdcution

The existence of dark matter is overwhelmingly supported by numerous cosmological and astrophysical observations on a wide range of scales. However, the nature of dark matter has not been revealed for almost a century except for its gravitational interactions. The identification of the nature of dark matter is one of the most important challenges of modern particle physics (see [1, 2, 3] for review).

Among various candidates for dark matter, the weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) are the most extensively studied category of dark matter. The WIMPs couple to the standard model particles via interactions similar in strength to the weak nuclear force. Through the weak interaction, the WIMPs are thermally produced in the early universe, and the relic density is set as they freeze out from the thermal bath [4]. The WIMPs are particularly attractive since the dark matter density does not depend on the details of the initial condition of the universe. The WIMPs are also highly motivated as they are interrelated to physics beyond the standard model such as supersymmetry (see e.g. [5]).

The ambient WIMPs can be directly detected by searching for its scattering with the atomic nuclei [6]. Given a circular speed at around the Sun of 239±5239\pm 5 km/s [7], the WIMPs recoil the nuclei elastically with a typical momentum transfer of qA∼100q_{A}\sim 100 MeV for the target nucleus mass of mN∼100m_{N}\sim 100 GeV.11 1 For a lighter WIMP than mNm_{N}, qAq_{A} is suppressed by the reduced mass between the nucleus and the WIMP. The recoil signatures are detected through ionization, scintillation, and the production of heat in the detectors (see [8, 9, 10] for review). To date, for example, liquid xenon detectors such as LUX [11], PandaX-II [12], and XENON1T [13] have put stringent exclusion limits on the spin-independent WIMP-nucleon recoil cross section.

In those experiments, it is usually assumed that the atomic electrons around the recoil nucleus immediately follow the motion of the nucleus. However, it takes some time for the electrons to catch up, which causes ionization and excitation of the recoil atom. The ionization and the excitation result in extra electronic energy injections into the detectors.22 2 The rates of the ionization/excitation are much smaller than 𝒪⁡(1){\cal O}(1). Besides, the same effects are expected in the nuclear recoil by neutron injections. Accordingly, those effects are almost always taken into account in detector calibration by the neutron sources automatically. The importance of such effects on direct detection experiments has been pointed out [14, *Moustakidis:2005gx, *Ejiri:2005aj, *Vergados:2013raa, 18]. (See also Refs. [19, 20], which discuss the ionization effects in the direct detection experiments for dark matter electron scattering.)

In previous studies, such effects are estimated by using the so-called Migdal’s approach [21, 22] (see also [23]). Following [18], we call these effects the Migdal effects. In the Migdal’s approach, a state of the electron cloud just after a nuclear recoil is approximated by

|Φe​c′⟩=e−ime∑i𝐯⋅𝐱^i|Φe​c⟩,\displaystyle|\Phi_{ec}^{\prime}\rangle=e^{-im_{e}\sum_{i}{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}|\Phi_{ec}\rangle\ , (1)

in the rest frame of the nucleus. Here mem_{e} is the electron mass, 𝐱^i\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i} the position operator of the ii-th electron, 𝐯\mathbf{v} the nucleus velocity after the recoil, and |Φe​c⟩|\Phi_{ec}\rangle the state of the electron cloud before the nuclear recoil. The probability of ionization/excitation is then given by

𝒫=|⟨Φe​c∗|Φe​c′⟩|2,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}=|\langle\Phi_{ec}^{*}|\Phi_{ec}^{\prime}\rangle|^{2}\ , (2)

where |Φe​c∗⟩|\Phi_{ec}^{*}\rangle denotes either the ionized or excited energy eigenstate of the electron cloud.

In the above analysis, the final state ionization/excitation are treated separately from the nuclear recoil. Thus, the energy-momentum conservation and the probability conservation are made somewhat obscure. In this paper, we reformulate the Migdal effect so that the “atomic recoil” cross section is obtained coherently. In our reformulation, the energy-momentum conservation and the probability conservation are manifest while the final state ionization/excitation are treated automatically. We also provide numerical estimates of the ionization/excitation probabilities for isolated atoms of Ar, Xe, Ge, Na, and I.

The Migdal effect should be distinguished from the ionization and the excitation in scintillation processes. The Migdal effect takes place even for a scattering of an isolated atom, while the latter occurs due to the interaction between atoms in the detectors. It should be also emphasized that the Migdal effect can ionize/excite electrons in inner orbitals, which are not expected in scintillation processes. As we will see, the ionization/excitation from the inner orbitals result in extra electronic energy injections in the keV range, which can enhance detectability of rather light dark matter in the GeV mass range.

The organization of the paper is as follows. In Sec. II, we discuss approximate energy eigenstates of an atomic state by paying particular attention to the total atomic motion. In Sec. III, we reformulate the atomic recoil cross section with the Migdal effect by taking the energy eigenstates in Sec. II as asymptotic states. In Sec. IV, we calculate the Migdal effect with single electron wave functions. In Sec.V, we estimate the probabilities of the ionization/excitation at a nuclear recoil. In Sec.VI, we discuss implications for dark matter direct detection. In Sec. VII, we briefly discuss the Migdal effect in a coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering. The final section is devoted to our conclusions and discussion.

II Energy Eigenstates of Atomic System

As we will see in the next section, the plane wave function of a whole atomic system plays a central role to obtain the nuclear scattering cross section with the Migdal effect. In the following, we consider an isolated neutral atom consisting of a nucleus and NeN_{e} electrons. The electrons are not necessarily bounded by the Coulomb potential of the nucleus, and hence, the energy eigenstates can be ionic states with unbouded electrons.

As typical nuclear recoil energy is smaller than 𝒪⁡(100){\cal O}(100) keV, the Hamiltonian of the system is well approximated by the non-relativistic one,

H^A≃𝐩^N22​mN+H^e​c​(𝐱^N)=𝐩^N22​mN+∑iNe𝐩^i22​me+V⁡(𝐱^i−𝐱^N).\displaystyle\hat{H}_{A}\simeq\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}+\hat{H}_{ec}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{N})=\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}+\sum_{i}^{N_{e}}\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{2}}{2m_{e}}+V(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{N})\ . (3)

Here, 𝐩^N\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N} and 𝐱^N\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{N} denote the momentum and the position operators of the nucleus with mass mNm_{N}, respectively. The momentum and the position operators of the ii-th electron are given by 𝐩^i\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i} and 𝐱^i\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}, respectively. The Hamiltonian of the electron cloud, H^e​c\hat{H}_{ec}, depends on the position operator of the nucleus, 𝐱^N\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{N}, through the interaction potential V^​(𝐱^i−𝐱^N)\hat{V}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{N}) (i=1⋯Nei=1\cdots N_{e}). The interaction potential also includes the interactions between the electrons. In the coordinate representation, the energy eigen-equation is reduced to

(𝐩^N22​mN+H^e​c​(𝐱N))​ΨE​(𝐱N,{𝐱})=EA​ΨE​(𝐱N,{𝐱}),\displaystyle\left(\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}+\hat{H}_{ec}(\mathbf{x}_{N})\right)\Psi_{E}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})=E_{A}\,\Psi_{E}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ , (4)

where the positions (including spinor indices) of the NeN_{e} electrons are represented by {𝐱}\{\mathbf{x}\} collectively.

II.1 Energy Eigenstates of an Atom at Rest

To solve Eq.(4), let us first consider the eigenstates of H^e​c​(𝐱N)\hat{H}_{ec}(\mathbf{x}_{N}) for a given 𝐱N\mathbf{x}_{N},

H^e​c​(𝐱N)​Φe​c​({𝐱}|𝐱N)=Ee​c​(𝐱N)​Φe​c​({𝐱}|𝐱N).\displaystyle\hat{H}_{ec}(\mathbf{x}_{N})\Phi_{ec}(\{\mathbf{x}\}|{\mathbf{x}_{N}})=E_{ec}(\mathbf{x}_{N})\Phi_{ec}(\{\mathbf{x}\}|\mathbf{x}_{N})\ . (5)

Since the system is invariant under spatial translations, the energy eigenvalues do not depend on 𝐱N\mathbf{x}_{N} while the wave functions depend on 𝐱N\mathbf{x}_{N} only through {𝐱i−𝐱N}\{\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{N}\};

Ee​c​(𝐱N)\displaystyle E_{ec}({\mathbf{x}_{N}}) =\displaystyle= Ee​c,\displaystyle E_{ec}\ , (6)
ΦEe​c​({𝐱}|𝐱N)\displaystyle\Phi_{E_{ec}}(\{\mathbf{x}\}|\mathbf{x}_{N})\ =\displaystyle= ΦEe​c​({𝐱−𝐱N}).\displaystyle\Phi_{E_{ec}}(\{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{N}\})\ . (7)

The eigenstates, ΦEe​c​({𝐱−𝐱N})\Phi_{E_{ec}}(\{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{N}\}), provide a complete orthogonal basis of the electron cloud for a given 𝐱N\mathbf{x}_{N}.

Next, let us show that ΦEe​c\Phi_{E_{ec}} well approximates an energy eigenfunction of the whole atomic system at rest, i.e.,

ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱})≡ΦEe​c​({𝐱−𝐱N}).\displaystyle\Psi_{E_{A}}^{(\rm rest)}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\equiv\Phi_{E_{ec}}(\{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{N}\})\ . (8)

By substituting ΨEA(rest)\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}} to Eq. (4), the energy eigen-equation results in

𝐩^N22​mN​ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱})=(EA−Ee​c)​ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱}).\displaystyle\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})=(E_{A}-E_{ec})\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ . (9)

Now, ΨEA(rest)\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}} (i.e. ΦEe​c\Phi_{E_{ec}}) depends on 𝐱N\mathbf{x}_{N} only through {𝐱−𝐱N}\{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{N}\}, the momentum of the nucleus is balanced with the electron momentum,

𝐩^NΨEA(rest)(𝐱N,{𝐱})=−∑iNe𝐩^iΨEA(rest)(𝐱N,{𝐱}).\displaystyle{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}}\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})=-\sum_{i}^{N_{e}}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}\,\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ . (10)

Thus, the left-hand side of Eq. (9) is expected to be highly suppressed, i.e.,

⟨𝐩^N22​mN⟩∼memN×Ee​c,\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}\right\rangle\sim\frac{m_{e}}{m_{N}}\times E_{ec}\ , (11)

for ΨEA(rest)\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}. Here, we used the fact that the expectation value of the electron kinetic energy is roughly given by

⟨𝐩^i22​me⟩∼Ee​cNe.\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{2}}{2m_{e}}\right\rangle\sim\frac{E_{ec}}{N_{e}}\ . (12)

Therefore, we find that ΨEA(rest)\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}} provides an approximate energy eigenstate of the whole atomic system with EA≃Ee​cE_{A}\simeq E_{ec};

H^A​ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱})≃Ee​c​ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱}).\displaystyle\hat{H}_{A}\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\simeq E_{ec}\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ . (13)

It should be noted that this is nothing but the Born-Oppenheimer approximation.33 3 In passing, Eq. (10) means that the state ΨEA(rest)\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}} is also an eigenstate of the total momentum of the atom, i.e. (𝐩^N+∑i=1Ne𝐩^i)​ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱})=0.\displaystyle\left({\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}}+\sum_{i=1}^{N_{e}}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}\right)\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})=0\ . (14)

II.2 Energy Eigenstates of a Moving Atom

Once we have the energy eigenstates of an atomic system at rest, the energy eigenstates of a moving atom with a velocity 𝐯{\mathbf{v}} can be immediately obtained by the Galilei transformation,

ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱})≃U⁡(𝐯)​ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱}).\displaystyle\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\simeq U(\mathbf{v})\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ . (15)

Here the unitary operator of the Galilei transformation is given by

U⁡(𝐯)=exp⁡[i​mN​𝐯⋅𝐱N+i​me​∑i=1Ne𝐯⋅𝐱i].\displaystyle U(\mathbf{v})=\exp\left[im_{N}{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{N}+im_{e}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{e}}{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}\right]\ . (16)

Under the Galilei transformation, the momentum operators are shifted by

U​(𝐯)†​𝐩^N​U​(𝐯)\displaystyle U(\mathbf{v})^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}U(\mathbf{v}) =\displaystyle= 𝐩^N+mN​𝐯,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}+m_{N}\mathbf{v}\ , (17)
U​(𝐯)†​𝐩^i​U​(𝐯)\displaystyle U(\mathbf{v})^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}U(\mathbf{v}) =\displaystyle= 𝐩^i+me​𝐯,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}+m_{e}\mathbf{v}\ , (18)

and the Hamiltonian is transformed into

U​(𝐯)†​H^A​U​(𝐯)=H^A+𝐯⋅(𝐩^N+∑i=1Ne𝐩^i)+12​m¯A​v2.\displaystyle U({\mathbf{v}})^{\dagger}\hat{H}_{A}U(\mathbf{v})=\hat{H}_{A}+{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\left(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}+\sum_{i=1}^{N_{e}}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\overline{m}_{A}v^{2}\ . (19)

Here we define the nominal mass of the atom by

m¯A=mN+Ne​me.\displaystyle\overline{m}_{A}=m_{N}+N_{e}m_{e}\ . (20)

By using Eqs. (13), (10), and (19), we find that the boosted wave function ΨEA\Psi_{E_{A}} satisfies,

H^A​ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱})≃(Ee​c+12​m¯A​v2)​ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱}).\displaystyle\hat{H}_{A}\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\simeq\left(E_{ec}+\frac{1}{2}\overline{m}_{A}v^{2}\right)\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ . (21)

Therefore, the boosted wave function ΨEA\Psi_{E_{A}} provides the approximate energy eigenstate of a moving atom with energy

EA≃Ee​c+12​m¯A​v2.\displaystyle E_{A}\simeq E_{ec}+\frac{1}{2}\overline{m}_{A}v^{2}\ . (22)

In summary, the eigenstate of the atomic system is approximated by

ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱})\displaystyle\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\}) ≃\displaystyle\simeq ei​𝐩N⋅𝐱N​ei​∑i=1Ne𝐪e⋅𝐱i​ΨEA(rest)​(𝐱N,{𝐱}),\displaystyle e^{i{\mathbf{p}}_{N}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{N}}e^{i\sum_{i=1}^{N_{e}}{\mathbf{q}_{e}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}}\Psi_{E_{A}}^{{\rm(rest)}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ , (23)
𝐩N\displaystyle{\mathbf{p}}_{N} =\displaystyle= mN​𝐯,\displaystyle m_{N}{\mathbf{v}}\ , (24)
𝐪e\displaystyle{\mathbf{q}}_{e} =\displaystyle= me​𝐯,\displaystyle m_{e}{\mathbf{v}}\ , (25)

with

EA≃Ee​c+12​m¯A​v2.\displaystyle E_{A}\simeq E_{ec}+\frac{1}{2}\overline{m}_{A}v^{2}\ . (26)

It should be remembered that ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱})\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\}) is not an eigenstate of the nucleus momentum 𝐩^N\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}. Instead, ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱})\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\}) is an eigenstate of the momentum of the whole atom;

(𝐩^N+∑iNe𝐩^i)​ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱})=(m¯A​𝐯)×ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱}).\displaystyle\left({\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}}+\sum_{i}^{N_{e}}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}\right)\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})=\left(\overline{m}_{A}{\mathbf{v}}\right)\times\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\})\ . (27)

Thus, 𝐩N{\mathbf{p}}_{N} in Eq. (23) parametrizes not the nucleus momentum but the eigenvalue of the total momentum 𝐩A=m¯A/mN×𝐩N=m¯A​𝐯{\mathbf{p}}_{A}=\overline{m}_{A}/m_{N}\times{\mathbf{p}}_{N}=\overline{m}_{A}{\mathbf{v}}. It should be also noted that the energy eigenstate in Eq. (23) is no more in the realm of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation for 𝐯≠0\mathbf{v}\neq 0 since they are not eigenfunctions of H^e​c\hat{H}_{ec} for a given 𝐱N\mathbf{x}_{N}.

III MIGDAL EFFECT : From Nuclear Recoil to Atomic Recoil

In this section, we derive the recoil cross section of the atomic system with the final state ionization/excitation.

III.1 Isolated Nuclear Recoil

Before proceeding further, let us first translate the dark matter-nucleus interaction in field theory to an interaction potential, which will be useful in the later analysis. For now, let us forget the electron cloud and take the nucleus as a free separated particle. In a relativistic field theory, the TT-matrix and the invariant amplitude of a scattering process are given by

TF​I=⟨𝐩NF​𝐩D​MF|𝐩NI​𝐩D​MI⟩=ℳ×i​(2​π)4​δ4​(pNF+pD​MF−pNI−pD​MI).\displaystyle T_{FI}=\langle{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{F}{\mathbf{p}}_{DM}^{F}|{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{I}{\mathbf{p}}_{DM}^{I}\rangle={\cal M}\times i(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{4}(p_{N}^{F}+p_{DM}^{F}-p_{N}^{I}-p_{DM}^{I})\ . (28)

Here, the plane waves of the dark matter and the nucleus are normalized by

⟨𝐩|𝐩′⟩=(2​π)3​2​p0​δ3​(𝐩′−𝐩),\displaystyle\langle{\mathbf{p}}|{\mathbf{p}^{\prime}}\rangle=(2\pi)^{3}2p^{0}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{p}^{\prime}-\mathbf{p})\ , (29)

with p0p^{0} being the relativistic energy of the particle.

As an example, let us consider a contact spin-independent interaction between a Dirac dark matter and nucleons;

ℒ=∑i=p,ngiM∗2​ψ¯i​ψi​ψ¯D​M​ψD​M,\displaystyle{\cal L}=\sum_{i=p,n}\frac{g_{i}}{M_{*}^{2}}\bar{\psi}_{i}\psi_{i}\bar{\psi}_{DM}\psi_{DM}\ , (30)

where M∗M_{*} denotes a mass parameter and gp,ng_{p,n} are dimensionless coupling constants. In this case, the squared invariant amplitude for the nucleus scattering is given by

|ℳ|2=16​mN2​mD​M2M∗4​(gp​Z+gn​(A−Z))2,\displaystyle|{\cal M}|^{2}=16\frac{m_{N}^{2}m_{DM}^{2}}{M_{*}^{4}}\left(g_{p}Z+g_{n}(A-Z)\right)^{2}\ , (31)

where ZZ is the atomic number, AA the mass number, and mD​Mm_{DM} the mass of the dark matter. The corresponding cross section is given by

σ¯N\displaystyle\bar{\sigma}_{N} ≃\displaystyle\simeq 116​π​|ℳ|2(mN+mD​M)2,\displaystyle\frac{1}{16\pi}\frac{|{\cal M}|^{2}}{(m_{N}+m_{DM})^{2}}\ , (32)
≃\displaystyle\simeq 1π​μN2M∗4​(gp​Z+gn​(A−Z))2,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\mu_{N}^{2}}{M_{*}^{4}}\left(g_{p}Z+g_{n}(A-Z)\right)^{2}\ , (33)

where μN\mu_{N} is the reduced mass,

μN=mN​mD​MmN+mD​M.\displaystyle\mu_{N}=\frac{m_{N}m_{DM}}{m_{N}+m_{DM}}\ . (34)

In the coordinate representation of quantum mechanics, the above invariant matrix element in Eq. (28) is reproduced by an interaction potential,

H^\displaystyle\hat{H} =\displaystyle= H^0+V^int,\displaystyle\hat{H}_{0}+\hat{V}_{\rm int}\ , (35)
H^0\displaystyle\hat{H}_{0} =\displaystyle= 𝐩^N22​mN+𝐩^D​M22​mD​M,\displaystyle\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}+\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{DM}^{2}}{2m_{DM}}\ , (36)
V^int\displaystyle\hat{V}_{\rm int} =\displaystyle= −ℳ4​mN​mD​M​δ3​(𝐱N−𝐱D​M),\displaystyle\frac{-\cal M}{4m_{N}m_{DM}}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{x}_{N}-\mathbf{x}_{DM})\ , (37)

with the initial and the final states

ψI​(𝐱N,𝐱D​M)\displaystyle\psi_{I}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\mathbf{x}_{DM}) =\displaystyle= 2​mN​ei​𝐩NI⋅𝐱N×2​mD​M​ei​𝐩D​MI⋅𝐱D​M,\displaystyle\sqrt{2m_{N}}\,e^{i{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{I}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{N}}\times\sqrt{2m_{DM}}\,e^{i{\mathbf{p}}_{DM}^{I}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{DM}}\ , (38)
ψF​(𝐱N,𝐱D​M)\displaystyle\psi_{F}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\mathbf{x}_{DM}) =\displaystyle= 2​mN​ei​𝐩NF⋅𝐱N×2​mD​M​ei​𝐩D​MF⋅𝐱D​M.\displaystyle\sqrt{2m_{N}}\,e^{i{\mathbf{p}}_{N}^{F}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{N}}\times\sqrt{2m_{DM}}\,e^{i{\mathbf{p}}_{DM}^{F}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{DM}}\ . (39)

Here, we normalize the initial and the final wavefunctions in conforming with the one in Eq. (29) with the relativistic energies approximated by their masses.

As another example, we may also consider a dark matter interaction with nucleons through an exchange of a light scalar particle, ϕ\phi, with mass mϕm_{\phi},

ℒ=−∑i=p,nyiϕψ¯iψi−yD​Mϕψ¯D​MψD​M,\displaystyle{\cal L}=-\sum_{i=p,n}y_{i}\phi\,\bar{\psi}_{i}\psi_{i}-y_{DM}\phi\,\bar{\psi}_{DM}\psi_{DM}\ , (40)

where yp,n,D​My_{p,n,DM} are Yukawa coupling constants. The invariant amplitude of the isolated nuclear scattering for each spin is given by

ℳ⁡(qN2)\displaystyle{\cal M}(q_{N}^{2}) ≃\displaystyle\simeq yD​M​(yp​Z+yn​(A−Z))​4​mD​M​mNmϕ2−t,\displaystyle y_{DM}\left(y_{p}Z+y_{n}(A-Z)\right)\frac{4m_{DM}m_{N}}{m_{\phi}^{2}-t}\ , (41)
t\displaystyle t ≃\displaystyle\simeq −qN2=−(𝐩NF−𝐩NI)2,\displaystyle-q_{N}^{2}=-({\bf p}^{F}_{N}-{\bf p}^{I}_{N})^{2}\ , (42)

in the non-relativistic limit. In the coordinate representation of quantum mechanics, the invariant amplitude is reproduced by adding a potential term

III.2 Invariant Amplitudes with Electron Cloud

Now, let us calculate the cross section of the nuclear recoil in the presence of electron cloud. For this purpose, we consider

H^tot=H^A+𝐩^D​M22​mD​M+V^int,\displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm tot}=\hat{H}_{A}+\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{DM}^{2}}{2m_{DM}}+\hat{V}_{\rm int}\ , (47)

in the coordinate representation, where H^A\hat{H}_{A} is given in Eq. (3). In subsection III.1, we considered the asymptotic states consist of the plane waves of dark matter and an isolated nucleus. To take into account the electron cloud, we replace the plane waves of the nucleus with the plane waves of the atomic system discussed in section II.

The initial and the final states of dark matter scattering are taken to be

EF\displaystyle E_{F} =\displaystyle= Ee​cF+m¯A2vF2+𝐩D​MF22​mD​M,\displaystyle E_{ec}^{F}+\frac{\overline{m}_{A}}{2}v_{F}{}^{2}+\frac{{\mathbf{p}}_{DM}^{F}{}^{2}}{2m_{DM}}\ , (51)

where Ee​cI,FE_{ec}^{I,F} are the energy eigenvalues of the initial and the final electron clouds in the rest frame, respectively. By using the energy eigenfunctions in Eq. (23), the TT-matrix of this process is given by

for 𝐯I=0\mathbf{v}_{I}=0.55 5 The Fermi’s golden rule is justified by taking the timescale much loner than (Ee​cF−Ee​cI)−1(E_{ec}^{F}-E_{ec}^{I})^{-1}. This timescale is also much longer than the typical radius of the electron cloud divided by the speed of light, and hence, the use of the electrostatic potential is also justified. It should be emphasized that our approach treats the nucleus and the electron cloud coherently. This treatment enables us to derive the invariant amplitude with manifest energy-momentum conservation.

IV Migdal Effect In Single Electron Approximation

IV.1 Single Electron Wave Function

In our numerical calculation, we use the electron wave function, ΦEe​c\Phi_{E_{ec}}, obtained by the Dirac-Hartree-Fock method, where the relativistic effects on the electron cloud are taken into account (see e.g. [28] for review).

In the Dirac-Hartree-Fock approximation, an electron state is given by a Slater determinant made up of one orbital per each electron in an averaged central potential around a nucleus. In this approximation, the energy eigenstates in Eq. (23) are approximated by

ΨEA​(𝐱N,{𝐱})\displaystyle\Psi_{E_{A}}(\mathbf{x}_{N},\{\mathbf{x}\}) ≃\displaystyle\simeq ei​𝐩N⋅𝐱N​∑σ∈SNesgn⁡(σ)Ne!​ei​𝐪e⋅𝐱1​ϕoσ⁡(1)α1​(𝐱1−𝐱N)​ei​𝐪e⋅𝐱2​ϕoσ⁡(2)α2​(𝐱2−𝐱N)\displaystyle e^{i{\mathbf{p}}_{N}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{N}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{N_{e}}}\frac{\rm sgn(\sigma)}{\sqrt{N_{e}!}}e^{i{\mathbf{q}}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1}}\phi^{\alpha_{1}}_{{o}_{\sigma(1)}}(\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{N})e^{i{\mathbf{q}}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{2}}\phi^{\alpha_{2}}_{{o}_{\sigma(2)}}(\mathbf{x}_{2}-\mathbf{x}_{N}) (78)
×⋯ei​𝐪e⋅𝐱Neϕoσ⁡(Ne)αNe(𝐱Ne−𝐱N),\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt\times\cdots e^{i{\mathbf{q}}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{N_{e}}}\phi^{\alpha_{N_{e}}}_{{o}_{\sigma(N_{e})}}(\mathbf{x}_{N_{e}}-\mathbf{x}_{N})\ ,

where SNeS_{N_{e}} denotes the permutation group of degree NeN_{e}. Here we explicitly show the indices of the Dirac spinor by αi=1⋯4\alpha_{i}=1\cdots 4, which are encapsulated in {𝐱}\{\mathbf{x}\} on the left-hand side.

The electron cloud consists of the NeN_{e} orbitals,1010 10 The Slater determinant in Eq. (78) is reducible in terms of the total angular momentum of the atom.

ec={o1,o2,⋯oNe},\displaystyle ec=\{o_{1},o_{2},\cdots o_{N_{e}}\}\ , (79)

where each orbital is specified by energy EE, relativistic angular momentum κ\kappa, and magnetic quantum number mm,1111 11 The value κ\kappa determines both the total angular momentum jj and the orbital angular momentum ℓ\ell via κ=∓(j+1/2)\kappa=\mp(j+1/2) for j=ℓ±1/2j=\ell\pm 1/2.

oi=(Ei,κi,mi).\displaystyle o_{i}=(E_{i},\kappa_{i},m_{i})\ . (80)

For a bounded electron, i.e. Ei<0E_{i}<0, the state is classified by the principle quantum number, nin_{i}, while the spectrum is continuous for an unbounded electron, i.e. for Ei>0E_{i}>0.

The one electron Dirac orbital ϕoα​(𝐱i)\phi_{o}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}_{i}) is given by using the two-component spherical spinors Ωκ​m\Omega_{\kappa m};

ϕo​(𝐱)=1r​(PE​(r)​Ωκ​m​(θ,φ)i​QE​(r)​Ω−κ​m​(θ,φ)).\displaystyle\phi_{o}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{r}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}P_{E}(r)\Omega_{\kappa m}(\theta,\varphi)\\ iQ_{E}(r)\Omega_{-\kappa m}(\theta,\varphi)\end{array}\right)\ .

See e.g. [28] for the details of the spherical spinors and the radial wave functions, PE​(r)P_{E}(r) and QE​(r)Q_{E}(r). Here, an atom is at rest and rr denotes the distance between the electron and the center of the potential. The one-electron states are normalized such that

∑α=14∫d3𝐱ϕo(𝐱)α∗ϕo′α(𝐱)={δn​n′​δκ​κ′​δm​m′(bounded)(2​π)​δ​(E−E′)​δκ​κ′​δm​m′(unbounded).\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha=1}^{4}\int d^{3}\mathbf{x}\,\phi_{o}(\mathbf{x})^{\alpha*}\phi_{o^{\prime}}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}\delta_{nn^{\prime}}\delta_{\kappa\kappa^{\prime}}\delta_{mm^{\prime}}&({\rm bounded})\\ (2\pi)\delta(E-E^{\prime})\delta_{\kappa\kappa^{\prime}}\delta_{mm^{\prime}}&({\rm unbounded})\end{cases}\ . (84)

In the Dirac-Hartree-Fock approximation, the electron cloud transition factor in Eq. (58) is rewritten by

ZF​I(𝐪e)=∑σ∈SNesgn(σ)∏i=1Ne∑αi=14∫d3𝐱iϕoσ⁡(i)Fαi∗(𝐱i)e−i𝐪e⋅𝐱iϕoiIαi(𝐱i).\displaystyle Z_{FI}({\mathbf{q}}_{e})=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{N_{e}}}{\rm sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{N_{e}}\sum_{\alpha_{i}=1}^{4}\int d^{3}\mathbf{x}_{i}\,\phi_{o_{\sigma(i)}^{F}}^{\alpha_{i}*}(\mathbf{x}_{i})e^{-i{\mathbf{q}}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}}\phi_{o_{i}^{I}}^{\alpha_{i}}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\ . (85)

In this approximation, the transition amplitude is given by the product of the transition amplitudes between the electron orbitals.

IV.2 Single Electron Excitation/Ionization

For an atomic recoil with a momentum transfer smaller than the hundreds MeV range, the factor |𝐪e⋅𝐱i||{\mathbf{q}_{e}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}| is expected to be small than 𝒪⁡(1){\cal O}(1) on the atomic scale.1212 12 For vF≃10−3v_{F}\simeq 10^{-3}, for example, qe≃0.5q_{e}\simeq 0.5 keV and hence |𝐪e⋅𝐱i|≪1|{\mathbf{q}}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}|\ll 1 even for a Bohr radius. Thus, we consider the Migdal effect at the leading order of qeq_{e}. At the leading order of qeq_{e}, only one electron can be excited/ionized, and hence, the initial and the final state configurations are

c​eI\displaystyle ce_{I} =\displaystyle= {o1,⋯,ok,⋯oNe},\displaystyle\{o_{1},\cdots,o_{k},\cdots o_{N_{e}}\}\ , (86)
c​eF\displaystyle ce_{F} =\displaystyle= {o1,⋯,ok′,⋯oNe},\displaystyle\{o_{1},\cdots,o_{k}^{\prime},\cdots o_{N_{e}}\}\ , (87)

where

Ee​cF−Ee​cI≃Ek′−Ek.\displaystyle E_{ec}^{F}-E_{ec}^{I}\simeq E_{k}^{\prime}-E_{k}\ . (88)

Hereafter, we assume that the initial electron cloud stays in the ground state, where all the electrons are bounded by the Coulomb potential of the nucleus. In the final electron state, ok′o_{k}^{\prime} can be either a bounded or an unbounded orbital.

At the leading order of qeq_{e}, the electron cloud transition amplitude is reduced to

ZF​I​(𝐪e)\displaystyle Z_{FI}({\mathbf{q}}_{e}) =\displaystyle= z𝐪e(Ek′,κk′,mk′|Ek,κk,mk)=−i∑αk=14∫d3𝐱kϕok′αk∗(𝐱k)(𝐪e⋅𝐱k)ϕokαk(𝐱k).\displaystyle z_{\mathbf{q}_{e}}(E_{k}^{\prime},\kappa_{k}^{\prime},m_{k}^{\prime}|E_{k},\kappa_{k},m_{k})=-i\sum_{\alpha_{k}=1}^{4}\int d^{3}\mathbf{x}_{k}\,\phi_{o_{k}^{\prime}}^{\alpha_{k}*}(\mathbf{x}_{k})({\mathbf{q}}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{k})\phi_{o_{k}}^{\alpha_{k}}(\mathbf{x}_{k})\ . (89)

At this order, electron transitions are allowed only when the orbital angular momenta of ok′o_{k}^{\prime} and oko_{k} differ by one, i.e. |ℓk′−ℓk|=1|\ell_{k}^{\prime}-\ell_{k}|=1. Thus, the transition amplitude is reduced to

z𝐪e(Ek′,κk′,mk′|Ek,κk,mk)\displaystyle z_{\mathbf{q}_{e}}(E_{k}^{\prime},\kappa_{k}^{\prime},m_{k}^{\prime}|E_{k},\kappa_{k},m_{k}) =\displaystyle= −iqe∫drr×[PEk′(r)PEk(r)+QEk′(r)QEk(r)]\displaystyle-iq_{e}\int dr\,r\times\left[P_{E_{k}^{\prime}}(r)P_{E_{k}}(r)+Q_{E_{k}^{\prime}}(r)Q_{E_{k}}(r)\right] (90)
×∫d​Ω​Ωκ′,m′†​(θ,φ)​cos⁡θ​Ωκ,m†​(θ,φ).\displaystyle{\times\int d\Omega\,\Omega^{\dagger}_{\kappa^{\prime},m^{\prime}}(\theta,\varphi)\cos\theta\,\Omega^{\dagger}_{\kappa,m}(\theta,\varphi)\ }.

Here, we take the quantization axis of the angular momentum corresponds to 𝐪e{\mathbf{q}}_{e}. The angle, θ\theta, is the one between 𝐪e{\mathbf{q}}_{e} and 𝐱e{\mathbf{x}}_{e}. The choice of the quantization is irrelevant for the final results as we take an average/sum the magnetic quantum numbers of the electrons in the initial/final states.

In the following discussion, we only require an accuracy of 𝒪⁡(10){\cal O}(10)% for the electron binding energies. For this accuracy, the bound state energies for given principal number and the orbital angular momentum are not distinguishable, and hence, it is useful to label the bound states by (n,ℓ)(n,\ell). Accordingly, the transition rates are also labeled by (n,ℓ)(n,\ell),

∑F|ZF​I|2\displaystyle\sum_{F}|Z_{FI}|^{2} =\displaystyle= |ZI​I|2+∑n,ℓ,n′,ℓ′pqed​(n​ℓ→n′​ℓ′)+∑n,ℓ∫d​Ee2​π​dd​Ee​pqec​(n​ℓ→Ee).\displaystyle|Z_{II}|^{2}+\sum_{n,\ell,n^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}p_{q_{e}}^{d}(n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime})+\sum_{n,\ell}\int\frac{dE_{e}}{2\pi}\frac{d}{dE_{e}}p_{q_{e}}^{c}(n\ell\to E_{e})\ . (91)

Here, |ZI​I|2≃1+𝒪⁡(qe2​⟨r⟩2)|Z_{II}|^{2}\simeq 1+{\cal O}(q_{e}^{2}\left\langle{r}\right\rangle^{2}) is the probability for the electrons unaffected by the nuclear recoil (see also appendix B for discussion of the probability conservation). The excitation and the ionization probabilities, pqedp^{d}_{q_{e}} and pqecp^{c}_{q_{e}}, are defined by

pqed​(n​ℓ→n′​ℓ′)\displaystyle p_{q_{e}}^{d}(n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= ωℓ′max−ωn′,ℓ′ωℓ′max​ωn,ℓωℓmax​∑κ,κ′,m,m′δℓ,|κ+1/2|−1/2​δℓ′,|κ′+1/2|−1/2\displaystyle\frac{\omega_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\max}-\omega_{n^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}{\omega_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\max}}\frac{\omega_{n,\ell}}{\omega_{\ell}^{\max}}\sum_{\kappa,\kappa^{\prime},m,m^{\prime}}\delta_{\ell,|\kappa+1/2|-1/2}\delta_{\ell^{\prime},|\kappa^{\prime}+1/2|-1/2} (92)
×|z𝐪e(En′​κ′,κ′,m′|En​κ,κ,m)|2,\displaystyle\times\left|z_{\mathbf{q}_{e}}(E_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}},\kappa^{\prime},m^{\prime}|E_{n\kappa},\kappa,m)\right|^{2}\,,
dd​Ee​pqec​(n​ℓ→Ee)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dE_{e}}p_{q_{e}}^{c}(n\ell\to E_{e}) =\displaystyle= ωn,ℓωℓmax∑κ,κ′,m,m′δℓ,|κ+1/2|−1/2|z𝐪e(Ee,κ′,m′|En​κ,κ,m)|2.\displaystyle\frac{\omega_{n,\ell}}{\omega_{\ell}^{\max}}\sum_{\kappa,\kappa^{\prime},m,m^{\prime}}\delta_{\ell,|\kappa+1/2|-1/2}\left|z_{\mathbf{q}_{e}}(E_{e},\kappa^{\prime},m^{\prime}|E_{n\kappa},\kappa,m)\right|^{2}\,. (93)

Here, En​κE_{n\kappa} is the size of the binding energy for the bounded electron labeled by (n,κn,\kappa), EeE_{e} the energy of the unbounded electron, ωn​ℓ\omega_{n\ell} the occupation number of the subshell (see Tab. 1), and ωℓmax=2​(2​ℓ+1)\omega_{\ell}^{\max}=2(2\ell+1). The final state orbital angular momentum, i.e. ℓ′=ℓ±1\ell^{\prime}=\ell\pm 1, is summed implicitly in Eq. (93).

IV.3 Ionization Spectrum at the Leading Order

By combining Eqs. (76) and (91), we find that the ionized electron spectrum from an initial orbital oko_{k} associated is given by

d​Rd​ER​d​Ee​d​vD​M\displaystyle\frac{dR}{dE_{R}\,dE_{e}\,dv_{DM}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq d​R0d​ER​d​vD​M×12​π∑n,ℓdd​Eepqec(nℓ→Ee),\displaystyle\frac{dR_{0}}{dE_{R}\,dv_{DM}}\times\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n,\ell}\frac{d}{dE_{e}}p^{c}_{q_{e}}(n\ell\to E_{e})\ , (94)
d​R0d​ER​d​vD​M\displaystyle\frac{dR_{0}}{dE_{R}\,dv_{DM}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq 12​ρD​MmD​M​1μN2​σ~N​(qA)×f~​(vD​M)vD​M.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\rho_{DM}}{m_{DM}}\frac{1}{\mu_{N}^{2}}\tilde{\sigma}_{N}(q_{A})\times\frac{\tilde{f}(v_{DM})}{v_{DM}}\ . (95)

Here,

ER≃qA22​mA,qe≃memA​qA.\displaystyle E_{R}\simeq\frac{q_{A}^{2}}{2m_{A}}\ ,\quad q_{e}\simeq\frac{m_{e}}{m_{A}}q_{A}\ . (96)

It should be noted that the atomic recoil energy, ERE_{R}, and the electron transition energy, Δ​E{\Delta}E, are correlated through the energy-momentum conservation;

ER\displaystyle E_{R} =\displaystyle= μN22​mN​vD​M2​((1−1−2​Δ​EμN​vD​M2)2+2​(1−cos⁡θC​M)​1−2​Δ​EμN​vD​M2),\displaystyle\frac{\mu_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}v_{DM}^{2}\left(\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{2{\Delta}E}{\mu_{N}v_{DM}^{2}}}\right)^{2}+2(1-\cos\theta_{CM})\sqrt{1-\frac{2{\Delta}E}{\mu_{N}v_{DM}^{2}}}\right)\ , (97)

where

Δ​E\displaystyle{\Delta}E =\displaystyle= Ee+En​ℓ,\displaystyle E_{e}+E_{n\ell}\ , (98)
En​ℓ\displaystyle E_{n\ell} =\displaystyle= 12​∑κδℓ,|κ+1/2|−1/2​En​κ.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\kappa}\delta_{\ell,|\kappa+1/2|-1/2}E_{n\kappa}\ . (99)

From this expression, we find the minimum dark matter velocity for given ERE_{R} and Δ​E{\Delta}E,

vD​M,min≃mN​ER+μN​Δ​EμN​2​mN​ER.v_{DM,\min}\simeq\frac{m_{N}E_{R}+\mu_{N}\Delta E}{\mu_{N}\,\sqrt{2\,m_{N}E_{R}}}\,. (100)

In Fig. 1, we show the minimum velocity as a function of ERE_{R} for isolated Ar and Xe atoms. We also show the kinematically allowed region of ERE_{R} and Δ​E{\Delta}E for Ar and Xe atoms for vD​M=10−3v_{DM}=10^{-3} in Fig. 2.

It should be also noted that there is a kinematical upper limit on the electron transition energy, Δ​E{\Delta}E, for a given speed of dark matter, which is set by Eq. (66),

Δ​EMAX=12​μN​vD​M2.\displaystyle{\Delta}E_{\rm MAX}=\frac{1}{2}\mu_{N}v_{DM}^{2}\ . (101)

In Fig. 3, we show Δ​EMAX{\Delta}E_{\rm MAX} as a function of vD​Mv_{DM}. The figure shows that Δ​E{\Delta}E in the keV range is kinematically allowed for vD​M≳10−3v_{DM}\gtrsim 10^{-3}. It is also notable that, for Δ​E=Δ​EMAX{\Delta}E={\Delta}E_{\rm MAX}, the atomic recoil energy is given by

ER=μN22​mN​vD​M2=μNmN×Δ​EMAX.\displaystyle E_{R}=\frac{\mu_{N}^{2}}{2m_{N}}v_{DM}^{2}=\frac{\mu_{N}}{m_{N}}\times{\Delta}E_{\rm MAX}\ . (102)

Thus the corresponding atomic recoil energy is smaller than Δ​EMAX{\Delta}E_{\rm MAX}, which plays an important role on the dark matter detections as discussed in the later section.

When electrons are emitted from inner orbitals, the created core-holes are de-excited subsequently.1313 13 The de-excitation proceeds through the X-ray transition, the Auger transition, or the Coster-Kronig transition (see [29, 30] for review, see also [31]). For a core-hole in n>1n>1 states the Coster-Kroning transition dominates the de-excitation process. The typical timescales of the de-excitation processes are of 𝒪⁡(10){\cal O}(10) fs. Thus, the energies of the electron emission and the de-excitation are measured simultaneously, and hence, the total electronic energy released at the ionization is given by

EE​M=Ee+Edex,\displaystyle E_{EM}=E_{e}+E_{\rm dex}\ , (103)

where EdexE_{\rm dex} is the energy released at the de-excitation.

Accordingly, the electromagnetic energy spectrum is given by

d​Rd​ER​d​EE​M​d​vD​M\displaystyle\frac{dR}{dE_{R}\,dE_{EM}\,dv_{DM}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq d​R0d​ER​d​vD​M×12​π∑n,ℓdd​Eepqec(nℓ→(EE​M−En​ℓ)).\displaystyle\frac{dR_{0}}{dE_{R}\,dv_{DM}}\times\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n,\ell}\frac{d}{dE_{e}}p^{c}_{q_{e}}(n\ell\to(E_{EM}-E_{n\ell}))\ . (104)

Hereafter, we simply assume that the ionization energy is released completely, that is EE​M=Δ​EE_{EM}={\Delta}E.1414 14 If the atom is completely isolated, the ionization and the subsequent Auger and Coster-Kronig transitions leave ionized atoms. In the medium, on the contrary, ionized atoms are also de-excited eventually. One caveat here is that EE​ME_{EM} is not the energy of a single electron/photon but the collection of the energies of the electrons and photons emitted at the de-excitation and the ionization. Thus, the detector responses to EE​ME_{EM} might be different from those to a single electron/photon with the same energy, although we do not take such effects into account in the following discussion.

Similarly, the excited atoms also lead to electronic energy release by de-excitation. Assuming the complete de-excitation again, we obtain the electromagnetic energy spectrum;

d​Rd​ER​d​EE​M​d​vD​M\displaystyle\frac{dR}{dE_{R}\,dE_{EM}\,dv_{DM}}\!\! ≃\displaystyle\simeq d​R0d​ER​d​vD​M×∑n,n′,ℓ,ℓ′pqed​(n​ℓ→n′​ℓ′)×δ⁡(EE​M−Δ​En​ℓ→n′​ℓ′).\displaystyle\!\!\frac{dR_{0}}{dE_{R}\,dv_{DM}}\times\!\sum_{n,n^{\prime},\ell,\ell^{\prime}}p^{d}_{q_{e}}(n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime})\times\delta(E_{EM}-\Delta E_{n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}})\ . (105)

Here Δ​En​ℓ→n′​ℓ′\Delta E_{n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}} is given by

Δ​En​ℓ→n′​ℓ′=12​∑κδℓ,|κ+1/2|−1/2​En​κ−12​∑κ′δℓ′,|κ′+1/2|−1/2​En′​κ′.{\Delta}E_{n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\kappa}\delta_{\ell,|\kappa+1/2|-1/2}E_{n\kappa}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\kappa^{\prime}}\delta_{\ell^{\prime},|\kappa^{\prime}+1/2|-1/2}E_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}\ . (106)

V Numerical Analysis

In this section, we provide numerical estimates of the electron transition probabilities, pqdp_{q}^{d} and pqcp_{q}^{c}, for isolated Ar, Ge, Xe, Na, and I atoms. To calculate the electron wave functions, we use the Flexible Atomic Code (FAC, cFAC) [32]. It is a multi-configuration Dirac-Fock (MCDF) program to calculate various atomic radiative and collisional processes. We give a brief review of the Dirac-Hartree-Fock method in appendix C. In FAC, all of the single electron wave functions, including those of excited and unboudend electrons, are calculated from a universal central potential,

V⁡(𝐱−𝐱N)\displaystyle V({\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{N}}) ≃\displaystyle\simeq VN​(r)+Ve​e​(r),\displaystyle V_{N}(r)+V_{ee}(r)\ , (107)
Ve​e​(r)\displaystyle V_{ee}(r) =\displaystyle= α​∑n,κωn​κ​ρn​κ​(r)​𝒬n​κeff​(r)r​∑n,κωn​κ​ρn​κ​(r),\displaystyle\frac{\alpha\sum_{n,\kappa}\omega_{n\kappa}\rho_{n\kappa}(r){\cal Q}^{\rm eff}_{n\kappa}(r)}{r\sum_{n,\kappa}\omega_{n\kappa}\rho_{n\kappa}(r)}\ , (108)

which is optimized for the (possible) ground state configurations. Here, VN​(r)V_{N}(r) denotes the Coulomb potential from the nucleus, and α\alpha the fine-structure constant. The factor 𝒬n​κeff{\cal Q}_{n\kappa}^{\rm eff} provides the effective charge of the central potential for the electrons in the n​κn\kappa-orbital;

𝒬n​κeff​(r)\displaystyle{\cal Q}^{\rm eff}_{n\kappa}(r) =∑n′,κ′ωn′​κ′​Yn′​κ′0​(r)−Yn​κ0​(r)\displaystyle=\sum_{n^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime}}\omega_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}Y_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}^{0}(r)-Y_{n\kappa}^{0}(r)
−(ωn​κ−1)∑k>0fk(κ)Yn​κk(r)\displaystyle\hskip 12.91663pt-(\omega_{n\kappa}-1)\sum_{k>0}f_{k}(\kappa)Y_{n\kappa}^{k}(r)
−∑n′​κ′≠n​κρn​κ,n′​κ′​ωn​κ​ωn′​κ′ρn​κ​ωn​κ∑kgk(κ,κ′)Yn​κ,n′​κ′k(r).\displaystyle\hskip 12.91663pt-\sum_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}\neq n\kappa}\frac{\rho_{n\kappa,n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}\omega_{n\kappa}\omega_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}}{\rho_{n\kappa}\omega_{n\kappa}}\sum_{k}g_{k}(\kappa,\kappa^{\prime})Y_{n\kappa,n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}^{k}(r)\,. (109)

Here, ωn​κ\omega_{n\kappa} is the occupation number of the subshell, ρn​κ=ρn​κ,n​κ,Yn​κk=Yn​κ,n​κk\rho_{n\kappa}=\rho_{n\kappa,n\kappa},~Y^{k}_{n\kappa}=Y^{k}_{n\kappa,n\kappa}, and

ρn​κ,n′​κ′​(r)\displaystyle\rho_{n\kappa,n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}(r) =\displaystyle= Pn​κ​(r)​Pn′​κ′​(r)+Qn​κ​(r)​Qn′​κ′​(r),\displaystyle P_{n\kappa}(r)P_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}(r)+Q_{n\kappa}(r)Q_{n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}(r)\,, (110)
Yn​κ,n′​κ′k​(r)\displaystyle Y_{n\kappa,n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}^{k}(r) =\displaystyle= r​∫r<kr>k+1​ρn​κ,n′​κ′​(r′)​d​r′,\displaystyle r\int\frac{r_{<}^{k}}{r_{>}^{k+1}}\rho_{n\kappa,n^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}}(r^{\prime})dr^{\prime}\,, (111)
fk​(κ)\displaystyle f_{k}(\kappa) =\displaystyle= (1+12​jκ)​(jκkjκ−1/201/2)2,\displaystyle\left(1+\frac{1}{2j_{\kappa}}\right){\small\begin{pmatrix}j_{\kappa}&k&j_{\kappa}\\ -1/2&0&1/2\end{pmatrix}}^{2}\ , (112)
gk​(κ,κ′)\displaystyle g_{k}(\kappa,\kappa^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= (jκkjκ′−1/201/2)2,\displaystyle{\small\begin{pmatrix}j_{\kappa}&k&j_{\kappa^{\prime}}\\ -1/2&0&1/2\end{pmatrix}}^{2}\ , (113)

where jκj_{\kappa} is the value of jj corresponding to κ\kappa, r>=max⁡(r,r′)r_{>}=\max(r,r^{\prime}), r<=min⁡(r,r′)r_{<}=\min(r,r^{\prime}), and (j1j2j3m1m2m3)\begin{pmatrix}j_{1}&j_{2}&j_{3}\\ m_{1}&m_{2}&m_{3}\end{pmatrix} is the Wigner 3​j3j symbol.

Due to the universal central potential, the wave functions of orbitals obtained by FAC are orthogonal to each other, and hence, they can be used to calculate the transition rates in the previous sections. In our analysis, we further approximate the atomic state by a single Slater determinant of the wave functions labeled by a set of {n,κ,m}\{n,\kappa,m\}. The energy eigenvalues obtained with this approximation reproduce the measured values in Ref. [33] at the accuracy better than 2020%, which is good enough for later discussion (see the energy levels in Tab. 2.).

V.1 Transition probabilities

We show the numerical results of the transition probabilities to the order of O⁡(qe2)O(q_{e}^{2}). The ground state of the atom consists of a complex of the orbitals given in Tab 1. If there are more than one energy eigenstate configurations for a given complex, we take an average of the transition probabilities for those energy eigenstate configurations. As discussed in section IV.2, we consider the final states in which only one of oko_{k}’s in the initial state is replaced by an excited or an unbouded electron state.

In Fig. 4, we show the differential ionization probabilities, d​pqec/d​Eedp^{c}_{q_{e}}/dE_{e}, for qe=me​vFq_{e}=m_{e}v_{F} with vF=10−3v_{F}=10^{-3}. In the figure, we sum all the contributions from different orbital angular momenta in the initial state, ℓ\ell, for a given principal quantum number, nn. We also sum all the possible final states for a given nn. It should be noted that the spectrum shape of d​pqec/d​Eedp^{c}_{q_{e}}/dE_{e} does not depend on vFv_{F}, and hence, the probabilities for a different qeq_{e} is obtained by multiplying qe2/(me×10−3)2q_{e}^{2}/(m_{e}\times 10^{-3})^{2}. The integrated probabilities are also given in Tab. 2 for a given initial (n,ℓ)(n,\ell). The results show that the ionization probabilities from the inner shells can be of 𝒪⁡(10−2){\cal O}(10^{-2}) for vF=10−3v_{F}=10^{-3}. The ionization probabilities from the valence electrons can be even of 𝒪⁡(10−1){\cal O}(10^{-1}).

As we have seen in Fig. 2, the recoil energy ERE_{R} and the electron excitation energy Δ​E{\Delta}E (and hence EeE_{e}) are kinematically constrained for given mD​Mm_{DM} and vD​Mv_{DM}. Cross correlations of the ionization probabilities between ERE_{R} and EeE_{e} are obtained by rescaling the results in Fig. 4 by qe2=2​me2​ER/mAq_{e}^{2}=2m_{e}^{2}E_{R}/m_{A} within the kinematically allowed region in Fig. 2.

In Tab. 2, we also show the excitation probabilities, pqed​(n​ℓ→n′​ℓ′)p_{q_{e}}^{d}(n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}). As the table shows, the excitation probabilities are much smaller than the ionization probabilities for a given initial nn.

Before closing this section, let us comment on the probability conservation in the single electron transition. As discussed in the appendix B, the single electron transition probability satisfies,

1ωn,ℓ​(∑n′,ℓ′pqed​(n​ℓ→n′​ℓ′)+∫d​Ee2​π​dd​Ee​pqec​(n​ℓ→Ee))=−punchanged​(n​ℓ)−poccupied​(n​ℓ).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega_{n,\ell}}\!\!\left(\sum_{n^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}p_{q_{e}}^{d}\!(n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime})\!+\!\!\!\int\!\!\frac{dE_{e}}{2\pi}\frac{d}{dE_{e}}p_{q_{e}}^{c}(n\ell\to E_{e})\!\!\right)\!\!=\!1\!-p_{\rm unchanged}(n\ell)\!-\!p_{\rm occupied}(n\ell)\ . (114)

Here, punchangedp_{\rm unchanged} and poccupiedp_{\rm occupied} are given in Eqs. (146) and (148), while the lefthand side corresponds to pex​(n​ℓ)p_{\rm ex}(n\ell) in Eq. (147) (see also Eqs. (92) and  (93)). In our analysis, we numerically checked that punchangedp_{\rm unchanged}, poccupiedp_{\rm occupied}, and pexp_{\rm ex} satisfy the probability conservation in Eq. (114).1515 15 Numerically, poccupiedp_{\rm occupied} is at the same order or even an order of magnitude larger than pexp_{\rm ex}.

In Ref. [18], the probability poccupiedp_{\rm occupied} (Pe​x​c,i1P^{1}_{exc,i} in Ref. [18]) is incorrectly defined, which is related to poccupiedp_{\rm occupied} in this paper by

poccupied|[15]=poccupied×(1−punchanged).\displaystyle\left.p_{\rm occupied}\right|_{\tiny[15]}=p_{\rm occupied}\times(1-p_{\rm unchanged})\ . (115)

Since punchanged≃1p_{\rm unchanged}\simeq 1, poccupied|[15]\left.p_{\rm occupied}\right|_{\tiny[15]} is much smaller than poccupiedp_{\rm occupied}. The ionization probability in Ref. [18] is, on the other hand, estimated by using the (incorrect) probability conservation,1616 16 The one electron transition probabilities in this paper correspond to punchanged=Pi​i1p_{\rm unchanged}=P^{1}_{ii}, poccupied=Pe​x​c,i1p_{\rm occupied}=P^{1}_{exc,i}, and Pb​o​u​n​d,i1=∑n′,ℓ′pqed​(n​ℓ→n′​ℓ′)/ωn,ℓP^{1}_{bound,i}=\sum_{n^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}p_{q_{e}}^{d}(n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime})/{\omega_{n,\ell}}.

pionization|[15]\displaystyle\left.p_{\rm ionization}\right|_{\tiny[15]} =\displaystyle= 1−punchanged−poccupied|[15]−1ωn,ℓ​∑n′,ℓ′pqed​(n​ℓ→n′​ℓ′).\displaystyle 1-p_{\rm unchanged}-\left.p_{\rm occupied}\right|_{\tiny[15]}-\frac{1}{\omega_{n,\ell}}\sum_{n^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}p_{q_{e}}^{d}(n\ell\to n^{\prime}\ell^{\prime})\ . (116)

Since we find poccupied≳pexp_{\rm occupied}\gtrsim p_{\rm ex} numerically, it shows that the ionization rates in Ref. [18] are overestimated.

VI Effects on dark matter direct detection

As we have shown in the previous sections, a nuclear recoil is accompanied by the ionization and the excitation of the atom through the Migdal effect. The electric energy released by the ionization and the de-excitation can be in the keV range when the incident dark matter velocity exceeds the threshold in Eq. (66).

In this section, we discuss how those electronic energy injections affect the dark matter signals at direct detection experiments. In our analysis, we have assumed isolated atoms. Thus, the results in the previous section are not directly applicable to the non-isolated atoms in liquid or crystals. For example, the energy levels of the valence electrons are affected by the ambient atoms by 𝒪⁡(0.1){\cal O}(0.1) eV.1717 17 For the energy levels of the valence electrons of the liquid Xe, see e.g. Ref. [34]. Furthermore, when the electronic band structure is formed in the medium, the excitations into the unoccupied state should be reinterpreted as transitions into the conducting band.

The ionization rates from the inner orbitals are, on the other hand, expected to be less affected by the ambient atoms. In fact, the binding energies of the inner orbital are much larger than eV, and hence, the relevant length scales for the transition factors, zez_{e}, are much smaller than the typical distance between atoms. Thus, the ionization spectrum in Eq. (94) can be applied rather reliably for the ones from the inner orbitals.1818 18 As it is highly difficult to quantify the uncertainties from the effects of the ambient atoms, it is desirable to test the Migdal effect experimentally via the low energy nuclear recoils with ER≪𝒪⁡(1)E_{R}\ll{\cal O}(1) keV. In the following, we confine our arguments to liquid Xe detectors.

VI.1 Migdal Effects on the Recoil Spectrum

In the absence of the Migdal effect, the liquid Xe detectors respond to the nuclear recoil roughly through the following steps [35, 36, 37]. After the nuclear recoil, the electron clouds are assumed to catch up with the nucleus immediately, so that the atom remains neutral. The recoil “atom” loses its energy through scattering with adjacent atoms in the medium where the inelastic scatterings involve the ionization and excitation of the atoms. These processes continue until the scattered atoms are thermalized. Eventually, a fraction of the initial recoil energy ERE_{R} is converted to the measurable electronic excitation while the rest is lost into the heat of the medium [38, 39, 40, 41].

This should be contrasted with the electron recoils caused by incident gamma or beta rays, where the entire recoil energy is transferred to the measurable electronic excitation. Conventionally, the calibrated nuclear recoil energy, En​rE_{nr}, and the electron equivalent energy, Ee​eE_{ee}, measured by the scintillation photons are related by 1919 19 See e.g. Ref. [42] for the details of energy scale calibration of the liquid Xe detectors.

En​r=Ee​eℒeff⋅SeSn.\displaystyle E_{nr}=\frac{E_{ee}}{{\cal L}_{\rm eff}}\cdot\frac{S_{e}}{S_{n}}\ . (117)

Here, ℒeff{\cal L}_{\rm eff} is defined as the ratio between Ee​eE_{ee} and En​rE_{nr} at zero drift field relative to 122122 keV gamma rays, which is ℒeff≃0.1−0.2{\cal L}_{\rm eff}\simeq 0.1-0.2 for En​r≲100E_{nr}\lesssim 100 keV [43, 44, 45, 46]. The quantities, SeS_{e} and SnS_{n}, are the scintillation quenching factors of electron and nuclear recoils due to the drift electric field, EdE_{d}, which are Se≃0.4S_{e}\simeq 0.4–11 [47] and Sn≃1S_{n}\simeq 1 [48] for Ed≤4E_{d}\leq 4 kV/cm, respectively.2020 20 For Ed=0E_{d}=0 kV/cm, Se=Sn=1S_{e}=S_{n}=1.

In the presence of the transition due to the Migdal effect, the nuclear recoil is accompanied by electronic energy injections in the sub-keV to the keV range. By ignoring the energy resolution of the detectors, the electron equivalent energy spectrum is given by

d​Rd​Edet​d​vD​M\displaystyle\frac{dR}{dE_{\rm det}dv_{DM}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq ∫d​ER​d​EE​M​δ​(Edet−qn​r​ER−EE​M)​d​Rd​ER​d​EE​M​d​vD​M,\displaystyle\int dE_{R}dE_{EM}\,\delta(E_{\rm det}-q_{nr}E_{R}-E_{EM})\frac{dR}{dE_{R}\,dE_{EM}\,dv_{DM}}\ , (118)

with qn​rq_{nr} being the conversion between En​rE_{nr} and Ee​eE_{ee} in Eq. (117) (see also Eqs. (103) and (104)). In the following, we include only the electronic energy injection caused by the ionizations as the excitation probabilities into the unoccupied binding energy levels are much smaller than the ionization probabilities.2121 21 Moreover, the excitation into the unoccupied binding energy levels are not well defined when the electronic band structure is formed in the medium.

In Fig. 5, we show the total electron equivalent energy spectrum for a given spin-independent scattering cross section of dark matter on nucleons through the contact interaction.2222 22 The nucleon-dark matter cross section σ¯n\bar{\sigma}_{n} is related to σ¯N\bar{\sigma}_{N} via, σ¯N=A2×μN2/μn2×σ¯n\bar{\sigma}_{N}=A^{2}\times\mu_{N}^{2}/\mu_{n}^{2}\times\bar{\sigma}_{n} for gp=png_{p}=p_{n}. Here, we assume a detector with Ed=0E_{d}=0\,kV/cm as in the single-phase experiment such as the XMASS experiment [49]. We also fix qn​r=ℒeff=0.15q_{nr}={\cal L}_{\rm eff}=0.15. We adopt the Helm form factor [8, 5]. The local dark matter density is fixed to a conventional value, ρD​M=0.3\rho_{DM}=0.3 GeV/cm3. The local circular velocity is also fixed to be vcirc=220v_{\rm circ}=220 km/s with the peculiar motions of the Earth neglected.2323 23 The annual modulation caused by the Earth’s peculiar motion can be significantly enhanced as of the inelastic nuclear scattering [50]. We also assume a Maxwell velocity distribution with the velocity dispersion, v0=220v_{0}=220 km/s, which is truncated at the Galactic escape velocity vesc=544v_{\rm esc}=544 km/s.

The figures show that the electronic energy from the ionizations can be larger than the maximum value of the (electron equivalent) nuclear recoil energy for a rather light dark matter. As discussed in the previous section, the shape of the energy spectrum of the electronic injections is not sensitive to the incident dark matter velocity as long as they are kinematically allowed. The nuclear recoil energy, on the other hand, depends on the dark matter velocity,

ER≃qA22​mA≲12​μN2mA​vD​M2,\displaystyle E_{R}\simeq\frac{q_{A}^{2}}{2m_{A}}\lesssim\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mu_{N}^{2}}{m_{A}}v_{DM}^{2}\ , (119)

which is suppressed for light dark matter. These features can be seen from the figures; the electronic energy from the ionizations are less sensitive to the dark matter mass, while the maximum nuclear recoil energy is sensitive.

Given a typical threshold of the electron equivalent energy of the liquid Xe detectors of about a keVee, the ionization from n=3n=3 provides a new detection channel for rather light dark matter. For example, with exposures of about 10510^{5} kg⋅\cdotdays, a few hundred events are expected for mD​M≃500m_{DM}\simeq 500 MeV and σ¯n≃10−36\bar{\sigma}_{n}\simeq 10^{-36}cm2 in the liquid Xe detectors.2424 24 For much lighter dark matter, the ionizations from nI=3n_{I}=3 require very fast dark matter (see Fig. 1), and hence, the event rate is highly suppressed due to the dark matter velocity distribution. Similarly, a few signal events are expected for mD​M≃5m_{DM}\simeq 5 GeV for σ¯n≃10−42\bar{\sigma}_{n}\simeq 10^{-42}cm2 for the same exposure. It should be noted that those signals are eliminated as background events in the conventional analysis of the dual-phase experiments. In those experiments, one needs different analyses to cover such signals (see e.g. [51, 52]).

For heavier dark matter, mD​M>𝒪⁡(10)m_{DM}>{\cal O}(10) GeV, on the other hand, the Migdal effect is submerged below the conventional nuclear recoil spectrum, and hence, does not affect the detector sensitivities. In principle, the additional electronic energy injections affect the so-called S2/S1 ratio in the dual-phase detectors. This is because the numbers of direct excitons Ne​xN_{ex} and direct ionizations NiN_{i} are different for the atomic recoil and the electronic recoil.2525 25 For the electronic recoil, the ratio is given by Ne​x/Ni≃0.06N_{ex}/N_{i}\simeq 0.06 [53], while it is Ne​x/Ni∼1N_{ex}/N_{i}\sim 1 [37, 40] for the atomic recoil. However, such effects should have been taken into account by the detector calibration by the neutron sources for a given momentum transfer.

Finally, let us compare the Migdal effect with the final state photon emission of the nuclear scattering [54] (see also [55]). Similarly to the Migdal effect, the final state emission is also a universal effect and irreducible. The expected rates are, however, subdominant compared with the Migdal effect for ERE_{R} in the keV range [56]. The Migdal effect should also be distinguished from the photon emissions in the inelastic nuclear scatterings which require a larger momentum transfer [24, 25].

VII Migdal Effects in Coherent Neutrino-Nucleus Scattering

As another application, let us briefly discuss the Migdal effects in the coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering (Cν\nuNS). In a similar manner to the dark matter scattering cross section, the differential cross section of the coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering with the Migdal effect is given by

d​σd​ER\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq ∑Ee​cFd​σC​ν​N​Sd​ER×|ZF​I​(qe)|2.\displaystyle\sum_{E_{ec}^{F}}\frac{d\sigma_{C\nu NS}}{dE_{R}}\times|Z_{FI}(q_{e})|^{2}\ . (120)

Here, σC​ν​N​S\sigma_{C\nu NS} denotes the coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering [57, 58, 59],

d​σC​ν​N​Sd​ER\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma_{C\nu NS}}{dE_{R}} =\displaystyle= |FA​(qA2)|2​QW2​GF2​mA4​π​(1−mA​ER2​Eν2),\displaystyle\frac{|F_{A}(q_{A}^{2})|^{2}Q_{W}^{2}G_{F}^{2}m_{A}}{4\pi}\left(1-\frac{m_{A}E_{R}}{2E_{\nu}^{2}}\right)\ , (121)

with GFG_{F}, sin⁡θW\sin\theta_{W}, NN, QWQ_{W} being the Fermi constant, the weak mixing angle, the number of neutrons N=A−ZN=A-Z, and the weak charge of the nucleus QW=N−(1−4​sin2⁡θW)​Z≃NQ_{W}=N-(1-4\sin^{2}\theta_{W})Z\simeq N, respectively. As in the previous section, the magnetic quantum numbers of the electrons in the initial/final states are averaged/summed. For given EνE_{\nu} and Δ​E{\Delta}E, the recoil energy is constrained in

Δ​E22​mA<ER<(2​Eν−Δ​E)22​(mA+2​Eν),\displaystyle\frac{{\Delta}E^{2}}{2m_{A}}<E_{R}<\frac{(2E_{\nu}-{\Delta}E)^{2}}{2(m_{A}+2E_{\nu})}\ , (122)

where the maximal recoil energy corresponds to the back-to-back scattering.

In Fig. 6, we show the total electron equivalent energy spectra for the Cν\nuNS for the pp and the 8B solar neutrinos. Here, we take the central values of the neutrino fluxes of the SFII-GS98 model given in Ref. [60]. The single-phase liquid Xe detectors are assumed as in the previous section with qn​r=0.15q_{nr}=0.15. The figures show that the nuclear recoil signal without the Migdal effect is below the energy thresholds of the current liquid Xe detectors, i.e. 𝒪⁡(1){\cal O}(1) keV. The signal of the ionization from nI=3n_{I}=3 is, on the other hand, above the energy threshold, a few events of which are expected with exposures of about 1010 ton⋅\cdotyears.2626 26 More detailed study including background estimation will be given elsewhere.

VIII Conclusions and Discussion

In this paper, we reformulated the Migdal effect at the nuclear recoil caused by a dark matter scattering and a coherent neutrino-nuclear scattering. In our formalism, we take the plane waves of the whole atomic system as the asymptotic states for the scattering process. The coherent treatment of the electron cloud makes the energy-momentum conservation and the probability conservation transparent. We also provide numerical estimates of the ionization and the excitation rates for isolated atoms of Ar, Xe, Ge, Na, and I by using the Flexible Atomic Code (FAC, cFAC) [32].

We also applied the results for the dark matter direct detections by taking a liquid Xe detector as an example. We showed that the ionization signals through the Migdal effect provide new detection channels for light dark matter with a mass in the GeV range. Since such signals are eliminated as background events in the conventional analysis of the dual-phase experiments, different analyses are required to cover such signals. For rather heavy dark matter, on the other hand, the Migdal effects are submerged below the conventional atomic recoil spectrum.

In our analysis, we have not studied detailed detector responses nor the precise treatment of the Migdal effects of the non-isolated atoms in liquid or crystals. For more precise estimation, detailed detector simulations are imperative. In particular, it is important to study detector responses to the energy released by the de-excitation of the core-hole. More theoretical efforts are also required for precise estimation of the Migdal effect in the medium.

We also note that it is an interesting future work to discuss whether the Migdal effect affects the direct detection experiments that mainly aim the electron recoil [61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69]. As the Migdal effect provides the electronic signals via the nuclear recoil, dark matter without electron recoil can be searched for by those experiments.

pex​(k)\displaystyle p_{\rm ex}(k) =\displaystyle= ∫⁡∑o​∈​e​cI⁡|⟨ϕo|ei​𝐪e⋅𝐱^|ϕok⟩|2≃∫⁡∑o​∈​e​cI⁡|⟨ϕo|𝐪e⋅𝐱^|ϕok⟩|2,\displaystyle\,\,\,\mathclap{\displaystyle\int}\mathclap{\textstyle\sum}\,\,\,_{o\cancel{\in}ec_{I}}\left|\langle\phi_{o}|e^{i{\mathbf{q}_{e}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{x}}}|\phi_{o_{k}}\rangle\right|^{2}\simeq\,\,\,\mathclap{\displaystyle\int}\mathclap{\textstyle\sum}\,\,\,_{o\cancel{\in}ec_{I}}\left|\langle\phi_{o}|{\mathbf{q}_{e}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{x}}|\phi_{o_{k}}\rangle\right|^{2}\ , (147)
poccupied​(k)\displaystyle p_{\rm occupied}(k) =\displaystyle= ∑o∈e​cI\{ok}|⟨ϕo|ei​𝐪e⋅𝐱^|ϕok⟩|2≃∑o∈e​cI\{ok}|⟨ϕo|𝐪e⋅𝐱^|ϕok⟩|2,\displaystyle\sum_{o{\in}ec_{I}\backslash\{o_{k}\}}\left|\langle\phi_{o}|e^{i{\mathbf{q}_{e}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{x}}}|\phi_{o_{k}}\rangle\right|^{2}\simeq\sum_{o{\in}ec_{I}\backslash\{o_{k}\}}\left|\langle\phi_{o}|{\mathbf{q}_{e}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{x}}|\phi_{o_{k}}\rangle\right|^{2}\ , (148)

up to 𝒪⁡(qe3){\cal O}(q_{e}^{3}). The probability poccupied​(k)p_{\rm occupied}(k) denotes the transition between the occupied orbitals. The single electron transition probabilities satisfy

punchanged​(k)+pex​(k)+poccupied​(k)≃∑o|⟨ϕo|ei​𝐪e⋅𝐱^|ϕok⟩|2=1.\displaystyle p_{\rm unchanged}(k)+p_{\rm ex}(k)+p_{\rm occupied}(k)\simeq\sum_{o}\left|\langle\phi_{o}|e^{i{\mathbf{q}_{e}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{x}}}|\phi_{o_{k}}\rangle\right|^{2}=1\ . (149)

To the order of 𝒪⁡(qe2){\cal O}(q_{e}^{2}), the total probabilities can be expressed by using the single electron transition probabilities,

𝒫unchanged+𝒫ex\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\rm unchanged}+\mathcal{P}_{\rm ex} ≃\displaystyle\simeq ∏i(punchanged​(k)+pex​(k)+poccupied​(k)).\displaystyle\prod_{i}\left(p_{\rm unchanged}(k)+p_{\rm ex}(k)+p_{\rm occupied}(k)\right)\ . (150)

Thus, we find that Eq. (149) guarantees the probability conservation in terms of the single electron transition probabilities. It should be emphasized that poccupiedp_{\rm occupied} plays an important role for the conservation of the probability. As is clear from the above argument, however, poccupiedp_{\rm occupied} is a part of 𝒫unchanged\mathcal{P}_{\rm unchanged}, and hence, it does not contribute to 𝒫ex\mathcal{P}_{\rm ex} up to 𝒪⁡(qe3){\cal O}(q_{e}^{3}).

Appendix C Dirac-Hartree-Fock Method

In this appendix, we briefly review the Dirac-Hartree-Fock method in the natural units (see [28, 32] for review). The Hamiltonian for the electrons is given by

H^e​c=∑jh^j+∑i<jα|𝐫^i−𝐫^j|,\hat{H}_{ec}=\sum_{j}\hat{h}_{j}+\sum_{i<j}\frac{\alpha}{|\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{i}-\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{j}|}\,, (151)

where

h^j=𝜶¯⋅𝐩j+me​(β−1)+VN​(|𝐫^j|).\hat{h}_{j}=\bar{\bm{\alpha}}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{j}+m_{e}(\beta-1)+V_{N}(|\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{j}|)\,. (152)

Here, we ignore the Breit interaction terms and

VN​(r)={−Z​α2​RN​[3−(rRN)2],r≤RN−Z​αr,r>RN,V_{N}(r)=\begin{cases}-\frac{Z\alpha}{2R_{N}}\left[3-\left(\frac{r}{R_{N}}\right)^{2}\right],&r\leq R_{N}\\ -\frac{Z\alpha}{r},&r>R_{N}\end{cases}\,, (153)

with α​me​RN=2.2677×10−5​A1/3\alpha m_{e}R_{N}=2.2677\times 10^{-5}A^{1/3}. The Dirac matrices 𝜶¯\bar{\bm{\alpha}} and β\beta are defined by

𝜶¯=(0𝝈𝝈0),β=(1200−12),\bar{\bm{\alpha}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&\bm{\sigma}\\ \bm{\sigma}&0\end{array}\right)\ ,\quad\beta=\begin{pmatrix}1_{2}&0\\ 0&-1_{2}\end{pmatrix}, (154)

where 𝝈=(σ1,σ2,σ3)\bm{\sigma}=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{3}) are the Pauli matrices.

We assume that the electron wave function for the ground state is approximately given by

Φ⁡(𝐫1,⋯,𝐫N)=∑σ∈SNsgn⁡(σ)N!​∏j=1Nϕoσ⁡(j)​(𝐫j),\Phi(\mathbf{r}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{r}_{N})=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{N}}\frac{\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)}{\sqrt{N!}}\prod_{j=1}^{N}\phi_{o_{\sigma(j)}}(\mathbf{r}_{j})\,, (155)

with

ϕo={En​κ,κ,m}​(𝐫)=1r​(Pn​κ​(r)​Ωκ​m​(θ,φ)i​Qn​κ​(r)​Ω−κ​m​(θ,φ)).\phi_{o=\{E_{n\kappa},\kappa,m\}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{r}\begin{pmatrix}P_{n\kappa}(r)\Omega_{\kappa m}(\theta,\varphi)\\ iQ_{n\kappa}(r)\Omega_{-\kappa m}(\theta,\varphi)\end{pmatrix}\,. (156)

Here we use nn and κ\kappa, instead of EE, to label the radial wave functions. We choose {oi}\{o_{i}\} to be one of the ground state configurations.2727 27 In FAC, a fictitious mean configuration with fractional occupation numbers is used if there are more than one ground state configurations.

The ground state wave functions are determined by the variational method. The expectation value of the Hamiltonian is calculated as

⟨Φ|H^e​c|Φ⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi|\hat{H}_{ec}|\Phi\rangle =∑j⟨ϕoj|h^|ϕoj⟩+∑i<j⟨ϕoi,ϕoj​|α|𝐫^0−𝐫^0′||​ϕoi,ϕoj⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\langle\phi_{o_{j}}|\hat{h}|\phi_{o_{j}}\rangle+\sum_{i<j}\langle\phi_{o_{i}},\phi_{o_{j}}|\frac{\alpha}{|\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{0}-\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}_{0}|}|\phi_{o_{i}},\phi_{o_{j}}\rangle
−∑i<j⟨ϕoj,ϕoi|α|𝐫^0−𝐫^0′||ϕoi,ϕoj⟩,\displaystyle\hskip 12.91663pt-\sum_{i<j}\langle\phi_{o_{j}},\phi_{o_{i}}|\frac{\alpha}{|\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{0}-\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}_{0}|}|\phi_{o_{i}},\phi_{o_{j}}\rangle\,, (157)

where hh is the same as hjh_{j} but operates on a single electron state. Here, the expectation values in the coordinate representation are give by

⟨Φ′|Φ⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi^{\prime}|\Phi\rangle ≡∑σ′,σsgn⁡(σ′)​sgn​(σ)N!​∏j=1N⟨ϕOPENoσ′​(j)′)|ϕoσ⁡(j)⟩,\displaystyle\equiv\sum_{\sigma^{\prime},\sigma}\frac{\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma^{\prime})\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)}{N!}\prod_{j=1}^{N}\langle\phi_{o^{\prime}_{\sigma^{\prime}(j)})}|\phi_{o_{\sigma(j)}}\rangle\,, (158)
⟨ϕo′|f⁡(𝐫^0)|ϕo⟩\displaystyle\langle\phi_{o^{\prime}}|f(\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{0})|\phi_{o}\rangle ≡∑α∫d3​𝐫0​[ϕo′α​(𝐫0)]∗​ϕoα​(𝐫0)​f​(𝐫0),\displaystyle\equiv\sum_{\alpha}\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{0}[\phi^{\alpha}_{o^{\prime}}(\mathbf{r}_{0})]^{*}\phi^{\alpha}_{o}(\mathbf{r}_{0})f(\mathbf{r}_{0})\,, (159)
⟨ϕo1,ϕo2​|f⁡(𝐫^0,𝐫^0′)|​ϕo3,ϕo4⟩\displaystyle\langle\phi_{o_{1}},\phi_{o_{2}}|f(\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{0},\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}_{0})|\phi_{o_{3}},\phi_{o_{4}}\rangle ≡∑α,β∫d3​𝐫0​d3​𝐫0′​[ϕo1α​(𝐫)​ϕo2β​(𝐫0′)]∗​ϕo3α​(𝐫0)​ϕo4β​(𝐫0′)​f​(𝐫0,𝐫0′).\displaystyle\equiv\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{0}d^{3}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{0}[\phi^{\alpha}_{o_{1}}(\mathbf{r})\phi^{\beta}_{o_{2}}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{0})]^{*}\phi^{\alpha}_{o_{3}}(\mathbf{r}_{0})\phi^{\beta}_{o_{4}}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{0})f(\mathbf{r}_{0},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{0})\,. (160)

By taking the variation for the coordinate of one of the orbital electrons, we obtain

0\displaystyle 0 =h^​ϕoj​(𝐫)+[∑i⁡(i≠j)⟨ϕoi|α|𝐫−𝐫^0||ϕoi⟩]​ϕoj​(𝐫)\displaystyle=\hat{h}\phi_{o_{j}}(\mathbf{r})+\left[\sum_{i(i\neq j)}\langle\phi_{o_{i}}|\frac{\alpha}{|\mathbf{r}-\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{0}|}|\phi_{o_{i}}\rangle\right]\phi_{o_{j}}(\mathbf{r})
−[∑i⁡(i≠j)ϕoi​(𝐫)​⟨ϕoi|​α|𝐫−𝐫^0|]​|ϕoj⟩−εoj​ϕoj​(𝐫)+h.c.,\displaystyle\hskip 12.91663pt-\left[\sum_{i(i\neq j)}\phi_{o_{i}}(\mathbf{r})\langle\phi_{o_{i}}|\frac{\alpha}{|\mathbf{r}-\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{0}|}\right]|\phi_{o_{j}}\rangle-\varepsilon_{o_{j}}\phi_{o_{j}}(\mathbf{r})+h.c.\,, (161)

where εo\varepsilon_{o} is a Lagrange multiplier to impose

⟨Φ|Φ⟩=1.\langle\Phi|\Phi\rangle=1\,. (162)

This is the so-called Dirac-Hartree-Fock equation and gives simultaneous differential equations for ϕoj\phi_{o_{j}}. The second and the third terms express the electron-electron interaction and can be seen as local and non-local potentials for ϕoj\phi_{o_{j}}, respectively, once ϕoi\phi_{o_{i}} are treated as mean fields.

Since the non-local potential is numerically demanding, the Slater approximation is often adopted to localize the potential [70, 71]. However, since it has incorrect asymptotic behavior, FAC uses an improved potential given in Eq. (108). From Eq. (161), we finally obtain,

(dd​r+κr)​Pn​κ​(r)\displaystyle\left(\frac{d}{dr}+\frac{\kappa}{r}\right)P_{n\kappa}(r) =(εn​κ−V⁡(r)+2​me)​Qn​κ​(r),\displaystyle=\left(\varepsilon_{n\kappa}-V(r)+2m_{e}\right)Q_{n\kappa}(r)\,, (163)
(dd​r−κr)​Qn​κ​(r)\displaystyle\left(\frac{d}{dr}-\frac{\kappa}{r}\right)Q_{n\kappa}(r) =(−εn​κ+V⁡(r))​Pn​κ​(r),\displaystyle=\left(-\varepsilon_{n\kappa}+V(r)\right)P_{n\kappa}(r)\,, (164)

with

V⁡(r)=VN​(r)+Ve​e​(r),V(r)=V_{N}(r)+V_{ee}(r)\,, (165)

which is solved iteratively for the ground state. As for the excited states and the unbouded states, the single electron wave functions are obtained by solving Eqs. (163) and (164) by using the potential in Eq. (108), which is iteratively obtained for the ground state.
